docs.title: Chapter 6: Understanding Garbage Collection
docs.text:
Book: Optimizing Java — Practical Techniques for Improving JVM Application Performance

Authors: Benjamin J. Evans, James Gough, Chris Newland

Chapter: 6 — Garbage Collection Algorithms & Collector Fundamentals

Status: Complete

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • Explain the two fundamental rules of garbage collection and why Rule #2 is absolute
  • Describe the mark-and-sweep algorithm: phases, data structures, and limitations
  • Understand HotSpot's object representation (instanceOop, mark word, klass word)
  • Explain how Compressed Oops reduce heap overhead on 64-bit JVMs
  • Articulate the Weak Generational Hypothesis and the generational heap layout
  • Explain how TLABs enable lock-free O(1) allocation via pointer bumping
  • Describe what premature promotion is and why it causes Full GC pressure

docs.title: 1. The Two Fundamental Rules of GC
docs.text:
All garbage collection algorithms — regardless of complexity — must satisfy exactly two rules:

flowchart LR
    R1["Rule 1\nAlgorithms MUST collect\nall garbage"]
    R2["Rule 2\nNo LIVE object may\never be collected"]

    R1 -->|"Safety overrides all"| R2

    style R1 fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style R2 fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff

Rule #2 Is Absolute

Violating Rule #2 — collecting a live object — leads to silent data corruption or segmentation faults. Every GC design decision prioritizes Rule #2 above throughput, latency, or any other concern. This is why GC algorithms are conservative by design.

Java's GC eliminates the two most catastrophic C/C++ bugs: dangling pointers (use-after-free) and double-frees. The tradeoff is runtime overhead and non-deterministic pauses.

docs.title: 2. Mark-and-Sweep — The Baseline Algorithm
docs.text:
The simplest correct GC algorithm follows three phases:

flowchart TD
    CLEAR["① Clear Phase\nClear mark bit on ALL\nobjects in allocated list"]
    MARK["② Mark Phase\nDepth-first traversal from\nGC Roots — set mark bit\non all reachable objects"]
    SWEEP["③ Sweep Phase\nWalk allocated list;\nreclaim unmarked objects\nback to free list"]

    CLEAR --> MARK --> SWEEP

    style CLEAR fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style MARK fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style SWEEP fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff

docs.title: GC Roots — Where Tracing Begins
docs.text:
GC roots are external reference anchors outside the target memory pool that point into it. HotSpot recognizes these root types:

Root Type Description Thread Stack Frames Local reference variables in each live thread's stack JNI References Local and global JNI handles from native code Registers Variables hoisted into CPU registers by JIT Code Cache Roots Pointers embedded in JIT-compiled native code Static Variables References stored in class metadata Class Metadata References from loaded ClassLoader data

docs.title: Limitations of Naive Mark-and-Sweep
docs.text:
1. Fragmentation — After sweeping, live and dead slots alternate in memory. Subsequent allocations for larger objects may fail even with enough total free bytes
  2. Stop-the-World (STW) — Mutator threads must stop during marking to prevent the collector from missing newly created objects or following stale references
  3. Pause scales with live set — The longer the traversal from GC roots, the longer the pause

docs.title: 3. HotSpot Object Representation — OOPs
docs.text:
HotSpot represents Java objects using C++ structures called Ordinary Object Pointers (oops). An instanceOop header has two machine words:

flowchart LR
    subgraph HEADER["instanceOop Header (64-bit JVM)"]
        MARK["Mark Word (64 bits)\nIdentity hash code\nLocking state flags\nGC age bits (0–15)"]
        KLASS["Klass Word (32-bit compressed / 64-bit)\nPointer to class metadata\n(vtable, method dispatch)"]
    end

    subgraph KLASS_DETAIL["klassOop (class metadata)"]
        VT["vtable\n(method pointers)"]
        MI["mirror\n(java.lang.Class instance)"]
    end

    KLASS --> KLASS_DETAIL

    style HEADER fill:#3d59a1,color:#fff
    style KLASS_DETAIL fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff

PermGen → Metaspace

  • Java ≤ 7: klassOop lived inside the Java heap in PermGen (fixed max size, notorious OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space)
  • Java 8+: Class metadata moved to Metaspace in native (C heap) memory outside the Java heap — eliminates PermGen OOMEs; limited only by OS memory

docs.title: Compressed Oops — -XX:+UseCompressedOops
docs.text:
On 64-bit JVMs, object references are 64 bits. With heaps < ~32 GB, HotSpot applies a 3-bit shift trick to compress references from 64 → 32 bits:

Physical address = CompressedOop × 8 + HeapBase

This saves enormous amounts of memory:

Structure Savings Klass word of every object header 4 bytes per object Every reference field in instances 4 bytes per field Every reference element in arrays 4 bytes per element

Default Behavior

-XX:+UseCompressedOops is enabled by default on 64-bit JVMs when heap < ~32 GB. Setting -Xmx above ~32 GB silently disables it, increasing heap usage by ~30%.

docs.title: Object Header Layout Summary
docs.text: Field Size Notes Mark Word 64 bits Always full native size Klass Word 32 bits (compressed) / 64 bits Points to class metadata Length Word 32 bits Arrays only Alignment Padding 0–4 bytes Word boundary alignment

docs.title: 4. The Weak Generational Hypothesis
docs.text:
The entire generational GC architecture rests on a single empirical observation:

flowchart TD
    subgraph HYPOTHESIS["Weak Generational Hypothesis"]
        H1["Most objects die young\n(bimodal lifetime distribution)"]
        H2["Very few old-gen objects\nreference young-gen objects"]
    end

    subgraph CONSEQUENCE["Architectural Consequence"]
        C1["Separate heap into generations\n→ collect young gen frequently\n(fast, cheap)"]
        C2["Collect old gen rarely\n(expensive, but infrequent)"]
    end

    HYPOTHESIS --> CONSEQUENCE

    style H1 fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style H2 fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style C1 fill:#e8933a,color:#fff
    style C2 fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff

docs.title: Generational Heap Layout
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph YOUNG["Young Generation"]
        EDEN["Eden\n(new allocations)"]
        S0["Survivor 0\n(survivors age 1-N)"]
        S1["Survivor 1\n(always empty)"]
    end

    subgraph OLD["Old Generation (Tenured)"]
        TENURED["Long-lived objects\n(survived N GCs)"]
    end

    EDEN -->|"Young GC"| S0
    S0 -->|"age threshold met"| TENURED
    S0 -.->|"swap roles"| S1

    style EDEN fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style S0 fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style S1 fill:#7b68ae,color:#fff
    style TENURED fill:#e8933a,color:#fff

Survivor spaces use a hemispheric strategy: one space is always kept 100% empty. On each Young GC, live objects are evacuated from Eden + active Survivor into the empty Survivor space, incrementing each object's GC age counter. One space is always completely empty — this is not wasted memory; it enables compaction for free.

docs.title: 5. Thread-Local Allocation Buffers (TLABs)
docs.text:
Shared-heap allocation would require thread synchronization on every new operation. TLABs solve this:

flowchart TD
    subgraph EDEN["Eden Space"]
        T1["Thread 1 TLAB\n[private, lock-free]"]
        T2["Thread 2 TLAB\n[private, lock-free]"]
        T3["Thread 3 TLAB\n[private, lock-free]"]
        FREE["Unallocated\nEden Space"]
    end

    style T1 fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style T2 fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style T3 fill:#7b68ae,color:#fff
    style FREE fill:#3d59a1,color:#fff

Allocation mechanics: 1. Each thread gets a private TLAB slice from Eden 2. Allocation = pointer bump — advance the next pointer by sizeof(object) — O(1), no locking 3. When TLAB fills, thread requests a new TLAB (requires brief lock) 4. TLABs are dynamically sized based on thread allocation history

TLABs Are Private at Allocation Time Only

After allocation, objects in a TLAB are immediately visible to other threads via normal memory visibility rules. TLABs only eliminate lock contention at allocation time.

docs.title: Allocation Escalation Waterfall
docs.text:
When TLAB runs out:

TLAB allocation (lock-free pointer bump)
  → New TLAB from Eden (brief lock)
    → Allocation directly in Eden outside TLAB
      → Young GC triggered
        → Direct allocation in Tenured (last resort — huge arrays)

docs.title: 6. Card Tables & Write Barriers
docs.text:
The Weak Generational Hypothesis assumes few old→young references. But some do exist. Young GC needs to scan them without scanning all of Old Gen:

flowchart TD
    subgraph CARDTABLE["Card Table (byte array)"]
        C1["Card 0\n512 bytes of Old Gen"]
        C2["Card 1\n512 bytes"]
        C3["Card 2 [DIRTY]\n512 bytes"]
        C4["Card N\n512 bytes"]
    end

    BARRIER["Write Barrier\n(JIT-inserted code)\ncards[ref >> 9] = 0"]

    OLD["Old Gen Object\nfield = new YoungRef"] --> BARRIER --> C3

    style C3 fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style BARRIER fill:#e8933a,color:#fff

Every time application code stores a reference from an Old Gen object to a Young Gen object, the JIT-inserted write barrier marks the corresponding 512-byte "card" in the Card Table as dirty:

// Write barrier pseudo-code (executed on every reference store)
cards[objectAddress >> 9] = 0;   // shift right 9 bits = divide by 512

During Young GC, only dirty cards are scanned for cross-generational references — not all of Old Gen. A 1 GB old gen = only 2 MB of card table to scan.

docs.title: Parallel Young GC
docs.text:
The default collector pair in Java 8: ParNew (young) + ParallelOld (old).

Young GC mechanics:

  1. Stop all application threads (STW)
  2. Scan GC roots + dirty cards in Card Table
  3. Evacuate live objects from Eden + active Survivor to empty Survivor space
  4. Objects exceeding MaxTenuringThreshold → promoted to Tenured
  5. Resume application threads

Young GC Pause is Proportional to Live Set — Not Dead Objects

A Young GC with 400 MB Eden and only 20 MB survivors is fast — it only copies 20 MB. Dead objects are simply abandoned (Eden is then reused). This is why high allocation rates with short lifetimes work well generationally.

docs.title: ParallelOld — Compacting Tenured
docs.text: ParallelOld is a fully STW compacting collector. It relocates all live objects in Tenured to the bottom of the region, creating a single contiguous free area. Pause time scales linearly with live set size and heap size — on large heaps (> 10 GB live set), pauses can reach tens of seconds.

docs.title: 8. Premature Promotion — The Critical Antipattern
docs.text:
Premature promotion occurs when short-lived objects are forced into Tenured because Survivor space overflows:

flowchart TD
    BURST["Allocation Burst\n1 GB/s for 200ms\n→ 200MB allocated"]
    EDEN_FULL["Eden fills\n(only 400MB Eden)"]
    SURVIVORS["100MB still alive\n(< 200ms lifetime)"]
    OVERFLOW["Survivor space = 50MB\n100MB > 50MB!"]
    PROMO["100MB short-lived objects\npromoted to Tenured"]
    FULLGC["Full GC triggered prematurely\nto reclaim Tenured"]

    BURST --> EDEN_FULL --> SURVIVORS --> OVERFLOW --> PROMO --> FULLGC

    style BURST fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style OVERFLOW fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style PROMO fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style FULLGC fill:#b71c1c,color:#fff

Case study from the book:

Metric Normal (steady-state) With Burst (premature promotion) Young GC 20 MB evacuated to Survivor 100 MB promoted to Tenured Tenured occupancy Stable Grows rapidly with dead objects Full GC frequency Rare Triggered prematurely Application impact Minimal Long STW Full GC pauses

Diagnosis: -XX:+PrintTenuringDistribution reveals the age distribution of survivors. If many age-1 objects are being promoted, Survivor space is too small.

docs.title: Questions Explored
docs.text:
• What are the two fundamental rules of GC, and what happens if either is violated?
  • How does mark-and-sweep work, and why does it cause fragmentation?
  • What is an instanceOop and what does each field in the header represent?
  • Why does CompressedOops save ~30% heap space, and when does it get disabled?
  • What is the Weak Generational Hypothesis and why does it justify generational GC?
  • How do TLABs enable lock-free allocation, and what is the escalation waterfall?
  • Why does the hemispheric Survivor space enable implicit compaction?
  • What causes premature promotion and how do Card Tables help Young GC performance?

docs.title: Chapter 7: Advanced Garbage Collection
docs.text:
Book: Optimizing Java — Practical Techniques for Improving JVM Application Performance

Authors: Benjamin J. Evans, James Gough, Chris Newland

Chapter: 7 — Advanced GC: Concurrent Algorithms, G1, CMS & Low-Latency Collectors

Status: Complete

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • Explain the 5 GC tradeoffs and why no single algorithm wins on all dimensions
  • Describe safepoints — how threads enter/exit them, and what TTSP (Time to Safepoint) is
  • Walk through tri-color marking and explain the invariant that makes it correct
  • Describe CMS's 6 phases and explain what causes Concurrent Mode Failure (CMF)
  • Explain G1GC's region-based architecture, Remembered Sets, and humongous objects
  • Understand Shenandoah's Brooks pointer mechanism for concurrent compaction
  • Compare ZGC/C4/Shenandoah at a high level (mechanism and tradeoffs)

docs.title: 1. The Five GC Tradeoffs
docs.text:
There is no GC algorithm that optimally satisfies all concerns simultaneously. The pluggable GC architecture exists precisely because different workloads optimize for different tradeoffs:

flowchart TD
    subgraph TRADEOFFS["The 5 GC Tradeoffs"]
        PT["Pause Time\n(duration of app interruption)"]
        TP["Throughput\n(app time / total time)"]
        PF["Pause Frequency\n(how often STW occurs)"]
        RE["Reclamation Efficiency\n(memory freed per cycle)"]
        PC["Pause Consistency\n(uniformity of pauses)"]
    end

    AXIOM["Fundamental Axiom:\nNo single GC can optimize all 5"]

    TRADEOFFS --> AXIOM

    style PT fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style TP fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style PF fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style RE fill:#e8933a,color:#fff
    style PC fill:#7b68ae,color:#fff
    style AXIOM fill:#3d59a1,color:#fff
Collector Best For Weakness Serial GC Single-threaded, small heaps (< 100MB) Single-threaded STW — unusable for production Parallel GC Throughput-first batch workloads Long STW pauses on large heaps CMS Web apps needing low-pause old-gen collection Fragmentation; Concurrent Mode Failure G1GC Mixed workloads with pause goals (default since Java 9) Still has STW pauses; RSet overhead ZGC Sub-millisecond pause requirements Higher memory overhead for load barriers Shenandoah Concurrent compaction; very large heaps CPU overhead for forwarding pointers

docs.title: 2. Safepoints — Cooperative Thread Suspension
docs.text:
GC cannot simply pause threads at arbitrary points — it must wait for all threads to reach a safepoint: a known-good execution state where the thread's internal data structures are consistent and the GC can safely read/modify the heap.

flowchart TD
    JVM["JVM Sets\n'Time To Safepoint' Flag"]
    THREADS["Application Threads\nPoll the flag"]

    subgraph AT_SAFEPOINT["Already at Safepoint"]
        BLOCKED["Blocked on monitor\n(sleeping/waiting)"]
        JNI["Executing JNI\nnative code"]
    end

    subgraph NOT_AT_SAFEPOINT["Must reach safepoint"]
        INTERP["Interpreter:\nchecks between every 2 bytecodes"]
        JIT["JIT code:\nchecks at method exits\n& backward loop branches"]
    end

    JVM --> THREADS
    THREADS --> AT_SAFEPOINT
    THREADS --> NOT_AT_SAFEPOINT

    style JVM fill:#3d59a1,color:#fff
    style BLOCKED fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style JNI fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style INTERP fill:#e8933a,color:#fff
    style JIT fill:#e8933a,color:#fff

The Two Rules of Safepointing

  1. The JVM cannot force a thread into a safepoint state — threads must cooperatively reach one
  2. The JVM can prevent a thread from leaving a safepoint state — once stopped, threads stay stopped

docs.title: Time to Safepoint (TTSP)
docs.text:
TTSP is the delay between the JVM signaling "stop" and all threads actually stopping. A long-running JIT loop with safepoint polls only at the back edge can inflate TTSP by many milliseconds, making observed pause times longer than the GC work itself.

TTSP Is Invisible Without Diagnostics

Use -XX:+PrintGCApplicationStoppedTime and -XX:+PrintSafepointStatistics to distinguish GC pause time from TTSP. A 100ms "GC pause" may be only 2ms of actual GC work and 98ms of TTSP.

docs.title: 3. Tri-Color Marking — Concurrent GC Without STW
docs.text: Tri-color marking is the theoretical foundation for concurrent GC: marking the heap while application threads keep running.

docs.title: The Three Colors
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    WHITE["⬜ White\nNot yet reached\n→ Candidate for collection"]
    GRAY["🔳 Gray\nReached, but children\nnot yet scanned"]
    BLACK["⬛ Black\nFully scanned — all\nchildren are gray or black"]

    WHITE -->|"GC root found"| GRAY
    GRAY -->|"all children scanned"| BLACK

    style WHITE fill:#e0e0e0,color:#333
    style GRAY fill:#9e9e9e,color:#fff
    style BLACK fill:#212121,color:#fff

docs.title: Algorithm Execution
docs.text:
1. Color all GC roots Gray; all other objects White
  2. Select any Gray node → color its White children Gray → color the node Black
  3. Repeat until no Gray nodes remain
  4. All remaining White nodes are garbage — reclaim them

docs.title: The Tri-Color Invariant
docs.text:
The Invariant That Must Never Be Violated

No Black object may directly reference a White object during concurrent marking.

If a Black→White reference exists, the White object will be collected even though it is reachable!

docs.title: The Mutator Race Condition
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph BEFORE["Before Mutation"]
        B1["⬛ Black A"]
        G1["🔳 Gray B"]
        W1["⬜ White C"]
        G1 --> W1
    end

    subgraph MUTATION["Mutator Thread Runs"]
        B2["⬛ Black A"]
        G2["🔳 Gray B"]
        W2["⬜ White C"]
        B2 -->|"A.ref = C"| W2
        G2 -.->|"B.ref = null (removed)"| W2
    end

    subgraph AFTER["After — Invariant BROKEN"]
        B3["⬛ Black A"]
        G3["🔳 Gray B"]
        W3["⬜ White C — WILL BE COLLECTED!"]
        B3 --> W3
    end

    BEFORE --> MUTATION --> AFTER

    style W1 fill:#e0e0e0,color:#333
    style W2 fill:#e0e0e0,color:#333
    style W3 fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff

Fix: Write barriers that re-gray modified Black objects when references change, or SATB (Snapshot-At-The-Beginning) which treats anything reachable at GC start as live.

docs.title: 4. CMS — Concurrent Mark-Sweep
docs.text: CMS was the first production low-latency HotSpot collector. It handles Tenured concurrently while ParNew handles Young Gen.

docs.title: The 6 CMS Phases
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    IM["① Initial Mark
(STW — very short)
Mark direct roots
into Tenured"]
    CM["② Concurrent Mark
(concurrent)
Tri-color traversal
of live object graph"]
    CP["③ Concurrent Preclean
(concurrent)
Pre-scan dirty card
table entries"]
    RE["④ Remark
(STW — longer)
Fixup from concurrent
phase mutations"]
    CS["⑤ Concurrent Sweep
(concurrent)
Sweep dead objects
into free-lists"]
    CR["⑥ Concurrent Reset
(concurrent)
Reset internal state
for next cycle"]

    IM --> CM --> CP --> RE --> CS --> CR

    style IM fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style CM fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style CP fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style RE fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style CS fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style CR fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff

STW phases (red): Only Initial Mark and Remark stop the world — both are very short. Concurrent phases (green): Run alongside application threads, consuming CPU.

docs.title: CMS Tradeoffs
docs.text: Pro Con Short STW pauses for old gen Uses ~50% of CPU cores for concurrent GC work Good for latency-sensitive web apps No compaction → fragmentation accumulates Shorter full GC cycles Higher memory overhead

docs.title: Concurrent Mode Failure (CMF) — The CMS Killer
docs.text:
CMF occurs when CMS cannot finish collecting before Tenured runs out of space:

flowchart TD
    subgraph CMF_CAUSE1["Cause 1: Allocation Pressure"]
        A1["Young Gen promotions overflow Tenured\nbefore CMS finishes sweeping"]
    end

    subgraph CMF_CAUSE2["Cause 2: Fragmentation"]
        A2["Total free space is sufficient\nbut no contiguous block fits the promoted object"]
    end

    FALLBACK["CMF Recovery:\nFull STW compacting ParallelOld GC\n(the worst possible pause)"]

    CMF_CAUSE1 --> FALLBACK
    CMF_CAUSE2 --> FALLBACK

    style CMF_CAUSE1 fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style CMF_CAUSE2 fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style FALLBACK fill:#b71c1c,color:#fff

CMF Is a Performance Disaster

CMF forces a fully Stop-the-World compacting collection of the entire heap — often multi-second pauses. CMS should be pre-emptively triggered at 60-70% occupancy using -XX:CMSInitiatingOccupancyFraction=65 (default 75% is too late for bursty workloads).

docs.title: 5. G1GC — Garbage First
docs.text: G1GC is the default collector since Java 9. It targets predictable pause times on heaps from 4 GB to 100+ GB by collecting the regions with the highest garbage-to-live ratio first — hence "Garbage First."

docs.title: Region-Based Heap Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph G1HEAP["G1 Heap (Non-Contiguous Regions)"]
        E1["Eden"] 
        E2["Eden"] 
        E3["Eden"]
        S1["Survivor"]
        O1["Old"]
        O2["Old"]
        O3["Old"]
        H1["Humongous\n(multi-region)"]
        H2["Humongous\n(cont.)"]
        U1["Unused"]
        U2["Unused"]
    end

    style E1 fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style E2 fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style E3 fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style S1 fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style O1 fill:#e8933a,color:#fff
    style O2 fill:#e8933a,color:#fff
    style O3 fill:#e8933a,color:#fff
    style H1 fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style H2 fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style U1 fill:#3d59a1,color:#fff
    style U2 fill:#3d59a1,color:#fff

Region sizing: HeapSize / 2048, rounded to the nearest power of 2 (1 MB to 64 MB). Can be set explicitly via -XX:G1HeapRegionSize.

docs.title: Remembered Sets (RSets)
docs.text:
Each region has a private RSet that tracks references pointing into this region from other regions:

Without RSets With RSets Must scan entire heap to find cross-region references Only scan the RSet of targeted regions Pause scales with total heap size Pause scales with number of targeted regions

docs.title: Humongous Objects — The G1 Performance Trap
docs.text:
Objects > 50% of region size are humongous objects stored in contiguous Humongous regions in Old Gen:

Humongous Object Problems

  1. Allocated directly in Old Gen — bypasses Eden and Young GC
  2. RSets are never populated for Humongous regions (too expensive)
  3. Can only be collected during concurrent marking or Full GC
  4. Trigger: Large byte arrays (e.g., HTTP request buffers, Kafka messages, JSON blobs)

Fix: Increase region size with -XX:G1HeapRegionSize so objects < 50% of the new region size become regular old-gen allocations.

docs.title: G1 Mixed Collection Cycle
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    IM["① Initial Mark\n(STW — piggybacked\non Young GC)"]
    CRS["② Concurrent\nRoot Scan\n(concurrent)"]
    CM["③ Concurrent Mark\n(SATB — concurrent)"]
    RM["④ Remark\n(STW — SATB fixup\nweak ref processing)"]
    CL["⑤ Cleanup\n(STW — accounting,\nRSet scrubbing;\nempty regions freed)"]
    MIX["⑥ Mixed GCs\n(STW — evacuate highest-\ngarbage regions)"]

    IM --> CRS --> CM --> RM --> CL --> MIX

    style IM fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style RM fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style CL fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style MIX fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style CRS fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style CM fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff

Floating Garbage: Objects that die during concurrent marking may be kept alive in the current cycle because they were reachable at SATB snapshot time. They are collected in the next cycle. This is accepted as a design tradeoff.

docs.title: 6. Shenandoah — Concurrent Compaction
docs.text:
Shenandoah (Red Hat) achieves concurrent compaction using a Brooks pointer (forwarding pointer) embedded before every object header:

flowchart LR
    subgraph BEFORE_RELOC["Before Relocation"]
        OBJ1["Brooks Ptr → self\nObject Header\nFields..."]
    end

    subgraph DURING_RELOC["During Concurrent Compaction"]
        OBJ2["Brooks Ptr → 0xNEW\nObject Header\nFields..."]
        NEW["New Copy\nat 0xNEW\nObject Header\nFields..."]
        OBJ2 -->|"CAS update"| NEW
    end

    BEFORE_RELOC --> DURING_RELOC

    style OBJ2 fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style NEW fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff

Concurrent compaction protocol: 1. Shenandoah decides to relocate object from region A → region B 2. Creates a copy in new TLAB 3. CAS (Compare-And-Swap) atomically updates the Brooks pointer from self to newAddress 4. If CAS fails (another thread won the race), discard the speculative copy — winner's pointer is used 5. All subsequent accesses through any reference find the new location via Brooks pointer

Shenandoah pauses: Only Initial Mark and Final Mark are STW — all compaction is concurrent.

docs.title: ZGC — Colored Pointers (Java 11+)
docs.text:
ZGC uses colored pointers: unused upper bits of 64-bit pointers carry metadata that enables concurrent relocation with a load barrier:

64-bit pointer layout (ZGC):
Bits 0-41:   Object offset (42 bits → up to 4 TB heap)
Bit  42:     Finalizable bit
Bit  43:     Remapped bit
Bit  44:     Marked1 bit
Bit  45:     Marked0 bit
Bits 46-63:  Unused

When an application thread loads a reference, the load barrier checks the colored bits and potentially remaps/heals the pointer before the memory access proceeds. This is what makes ZGC achieve sub-millisecond pauses.

docs.title: Azul C4 — Loaded Value Barrier
docs.text:
The commercial Azul Zing JVM's Continuously Concurrent Compacting Collector (C4) uses a Loaded Value Barrier (LVB) — a self-healing read barrier that transparently updates relocated object references at the point of first access.

Object headers in C4 are a single 64-bit word (vs HotSpot's 2 words), saving 8 bytes per object.

docs.title: IBM J9 Balanced Collector — Arraylets
docs.text:
J9's Balanced Collector uses arraylets to handle large arrays in a region-based heap:

  • Large arrays are split into a spine object (array of pointers) and separate array leaves (actual data)
  • Leaves can reside in different regions — no need for contiguous memory
  • Enables NUMA-aware placement of array leaves near the threads accessing them

docs.title: 8. Epsilon GC — The No-Op Collector
docs.text:
Epsilon GC is a special-purpose collector that: - Allocates memory normally - Never collects garbage - JVM crashes when heap is exhausted

Use cases: 1. Microbenchmark isolation — Prevents GC from interfering with JMH measurements 2. Allocation rate profiling — Observe pure allocation behavior without GC noise 3. Short-lived processes — CLI tools that run and exit before filling the heap

docs.text:

  • What is a safepoint and why can't the JVM force threads into them?

  • How does tri-color marking enable concurrent GC, and what invariant must be maintained?

docs.title: Chapter 8: GC Logging, Monitoring, Tuning & Tools
docs.text:
Book: Optimizing Java — Practical Techniques for Improving JVM Application Performance

Authors: Benjamin J. Evans, James Gough, Chris Newland

Chapter: 8 — GC Logging, Monitoring, Tuning and Tools

Status: Complete

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • Configure mandatory GC logging flags for production JVMs
  • Explain why GC logs are superior to JMX for GC monitoring
  • Perform live incident triage to confirm/eliminate GC as the root cause
  • Apply the 4 core GC tuning factors to select the right approach
  • Tune Parallel GC, CMS, and G1GC with specific flag strategies
  • Understand the 1 GB/s allocation limit and its implication for tuning
  • Use jHiccup to measure JVM-level stall latency distributions

docs.title: 1. GC Logging — Mandatory for Every Production JVM
docs.text:
Non-Negotiable Production Requirement

Every production JVM process must generate a GC log in a dedicated file. GC logging is asynchronous, non-blocking, and adds ~0% performance overhead. There is no excuse not to enable it.

docs.title: Java 8 GC Logging Flags
docs.text:
# The complete mandatory GC logging configuration for Java 8
-Xloggc:/var/log/myapp/gc.log
-XX:+PrintGCDetails
-XX:+PrintTenuringDistribution
-XX:+PrintGCTimeStamps
-XX:+PrintGCDateStamps
-XX:+UseGCLogFileRotation
-XX:NumberOfGCLogFiles=10
-XX:GCLogFileSize=50m
Flag Purpose -Xloggc Write to dedicated file (not stdout) -XX:+PrintGCDetails Full per-phase timing breakdown -XX:+PrintTenuringDistribution Age histogram — reveals premature promotion -XX:+PrintGCTimeStamps Seconds since JVM start (correlate with JVM events) -XX:+PrintGCDateStamps Wallclock timestamps (correlate with app logs)

Log Volume Estimate

30 minutes at 50 MB/s allocation rate → ~600 KB of GC logs. Size your rotation accordingly.

docs.title: 2. GC Logs vs JMX — Why Logs Win
docs.text:
JMX is the wrong tool for GC monitoring:

Concern GC Logs JMX Data completeness Every GC event captured Sampling-based — misses events Heap accuracy Exact before/after occupancy Sampled snapshot only Overhead ~0% (async file write) High — RMI proxies + serialization Metric count > 50 metrics per event < 10 memory metrics Finalization trap None RMI teardown forces hourly Full GCs!

JMX Full GC Side Effect

RMI (used by JMX) has a built-in finalizer-based cleanup that triggers a Full GC once per hour by default (sun.rmi.dgc.server.gcInterval=3600000). If you see unexplained hourly Full GCs, JMX monitoring is likely the cause.

docs.title: 3. Live Incident Triage — The GC Diagnostic Flowchart
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    SLOW["Application is slow\nor unresponsive"]
    CPU["Check CPU Utilization\n(top / vmstat)"]
    HIGH_CPU["CPU near 100%?"]
    USER["User-space CPU > 90%?"]
    GC_LOG["GC log shows continuous\nGC activity?"]
    GC_ISSUE["✅ GC is the bottleneck\nProceed with GC tuning"]
    NOT_GC["❌ Not a GC issue\nInvestigate I/O, locks, external calls"]

    SLOW --> CPU --> HIGH_CPU
    HIGH_CPU -->|"Yes"| USER
    HIGH_CPU -->|"No"| NOT_GC
    USER -->|"Yes"| GC_LOG
    USER -->|"No (kernel CPU)"| NOT_GC
    GC_LOG -->|"Yes"| GC_ISSUE
    GC_LOG -->|"No"| NOT_GC

    style GC_ISSUE fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style NOT_GC fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style SLOW fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff

The Triage Triad: 100% CPU + >90% user-space CPU + active GC log = confirmed GC bottleneck.

docs.title: 4. GC Log Analysis Tools
docs.text:
Tool Type Best For Censum (jClarity) Commercial desktop/SaaS Automated analytics: premature promotion, spiky allocation, memory leaks, capacity planning GCViewer Open-source desktop Heap usage graphs, pause time visualization GCEasy Online SaaS Quick upload-and-analyze for one-off analysis

Never Write Custom GC Log Parsers

GC log formats are undocumented, non-standardized, and change between JDK minor releases. Hand-rolled parsers break silently on JDK updates. Always use established tools.

docs.title: 5. The Four GC Tuning Factors
docs.text:
Every GC tuning decision is driven by four application characteristics:

flowchart TD
    subgraph FACTORS["4 Core GC Tuning Factors"]
        AR["Allocation Rate\n(MB/s created by app)"]
        PS["Pause Sensitivity\n(max acceptable STW pause)"]
        TB["Throughput Behavior\n(batch vs interactive)"]
        OL["Object Lifetime\n(short-lived vs long-lived ratio)"]
    end

    SELECT["Collector + Configuration Selection"]

    FACTORS --> SELECT

    style AR fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style PS fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style TB fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style OL fill:#e8933a,color:#fff

docs.title: The 1 GB/s Allocation Wall
docs.text:
The Tuning Ceiling

Sustained allocation rates > 1 GB/s cannot be solved by GC tuning alone. No amount of GC configuration can outrun an application creating garbage faster than hardware can collect it.

The only solution at > 1 GB/s is application refactoring: eliminate object creation, use object pools, reduce boxing, avoid string concatenation in hot paths.

docs.title: Pause Sensitivity Bands — Collector Selection
docs.text: Application Type Max Pause Target Recommended Collector Batch / ETL / MapReduce > 1 second OK Parallel GC Web applications / REST APIs 100 ms – 1 s G1GC Low-latency services < 100 ms CMS / G1GC Ultra-low-latency / HFT < 10 ms ZGC / Shenandoah

docs.title: 6. Understanding Allocation Hotspots
docs.text:
Common sources of excessive allocation in Java applications:

Source Description Debug logging log.debug("Processing " + request.id) — string concat even if DEBUG is off Auto-boxing Map<String, Integer> boxing primitive int → Integer on every put Domain objects Order/Trade objects not being pooled or reused Framework overhead Spring/Jackson/Hibernate creating intermediate objects on every request

Top heap histogram entries in most Java apps (from jmap -histo):

 num     #instances         #bytes  class name
   1:      15234891     1828186920  [C                   (char arrays — String data)
   2:       7823456      939614720  [B                   (byte arrays — binary data)
   3:       6234123      748094760  java.lang.String
   4:       4532011      544441320  java.util.HashMap$Entry
   5:       2341234      281347680  [Ljava.lang.Object;  (Object arrays)

docs.title: 7. Heap Sizing — The Foundation of GC Tuning
docs.text:
# Production heap sizing
-Xms4g        # Initial heap size
-Xmx4g        # Maximum heap size (set equal to -Xms to eliminate resize pauses)
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m   # Cap Metaspace (Java 8+)

Always Set -Xms = -Xmx in Production

If Xms < Xmx, HotSpot resizes the heap dynamically, which triggers Full GCs. Set them equal to eliminate heap resizing pauses entirely.

docs.title: Card Table Scanning Math
docs.text:
The card table imposes a hard lower bound on Young GC pause times for large heaps:

Card table size = Old Gen size / 512 bytes per card

Example:
  20 GB heap with 15 GB Old Gen
  → 15 GB / 512 = 30 MB card table
  → Single-threaded scan of 30 MB card table ≈ 10 ms minimum

Result: Young GC on a 20 GB heap can NEVER be faster than ~10ms,
        regardless of how few objects survive.

docs.title: Tuning Parallel GC
docs.text:
Simplest collector — optimal for heaps < 4 GB where STW pauses are acceptable.

# Explicit sizing (legacy approach)
-XX:NewRatio=3      # OldGen:YoungGen = 3:1  → YoungGen = 25% of heap
-XX:SurvivorRatio=8 # Eden:Survivor = 8:1:1  → Eden = 80% of YoungGen

# Tenuring configuration
-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=15    # Max GC cycles before promotion (default 4)
-XX:PretenureSizeThreshold=1m  # Objects > 1MB go straight to Old Gen

Modern recommendation: Let the JVM ergonomically size generations — manual ratio tuning is rarely beneficial.

docs.title: Tuning CMS
docs.text:
# Trigger CMS earlier to prevent CMF
-XX:CMSInitiatingOccupancyFraction=65   # Start at 65% (default 75% is too late for bursty apps)
-XX:+UseCMSInitiatingOccupancyOnly      # Disable adaptive occupancy (use fixed fraction)

# Thread allocation
-XX:ConcGCThreads=4   # Concurrent GC threads (default: 25% of available cores)

# Fragmentation diagnostics
-XX:PrintFLSStatistics=1   # Log free-list statistics (detects fragmentation-CMF)

Signs of CMF approaching: - Back-to-back CMS cycles (CMS restarts immediately after completing — throughput drops 50%) - Free-list max chunk size shrinking over time - Promotion failures in GC logs

docs.title: Tuning G1GC
docs.text:
# Core G1 tuning
-XX:+UseG1GC
-Xmx32g -Xms32g
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200           # Pause target (hint, not guarantee)
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m           # Larger regions = less humongous object issues

# For high allocation rate workloads
-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=15        # Keep objects in young gen longer
-XX:G1NewSizePercent=40            # Larger young gen → fewer promotions
-XX:G1MaxNewSizePercent=60

# Diagnostics
-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions

G1 Tuning Philosophy:

flowchart TD
    PAUSE["Set MaxGCPauseMillis\nbased on app SLA"]
    HEAP["Set Xmx large enough\nfor live set + headroom"]
    REGION["Set G1HeapRegionSize to\navoid humongous objects"]
    YOUNG["Tune G1NewSizePercent\nfor allocation rate"]
    MONITOR["Monitor GC logs\nfor Full GC events"]

    PAUSE --> HEAP --> REGION --> YOUNG --> MONITOR
    MONITOR -->|"Full GCs still occurring?"| REGION

    style PAUSE fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style HEAP fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style REGION fill:#e8933a,color:#fff
    style YOUNG fill:#7b68ae,color:#fff
    style MONITOR fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff

docs.title: 9. jHiccup — Measuring JVM Stall Latency
docs.text:
jHiccup (by Gil Tene, Azul Systems) measures JVM-level latency stalls — not just GC pauses, but any JVM stoppage: GC STW, OS scheduling preemption, hypervisor pauses, JIT compilation hiccups.

# Attach to running process
jHiccup -p <pid>

# Or as Java Agent
java -javaagent:jHiccup.jar="-d 0 -i 1000 -l hiccup.hlog" -jar myapp.jar

# Process the log
jHiccupLogProcessor -i hiccup.hlog -o hiccup-results.hgrm

# Output: HdrHistogram percentile distribution
# Value at 50th percentile: 0.23 ms
# Value at 99th percentile: 2.1 ms
# Value at 99.9th percentile: 47.3 ms   ← GC pause visible here
# Value at 99.99th percentile: 234 ms

jHiccup vs GC Logs

GC logs tell you pause duration as measured by the GC subsystem. jHiccup measures the actual wall-clock stall experienced by application threads — it captures TTSP overhead, OS scheduling delays, and all other sources of JVM latency.

docs.title: GC Tuning Checklist
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["Enable GC logging\n(mandatory, zero overhead)"]
    B["Confirm GC is the bottleneck\n(Triage Triad)"]
    C["Check allocation rate\n(> 1 GB/s → code changes first)"]
    D["Check live set growth\n(growing → memory leak)"]
    E["Select collector based on\npause sensitivity"]
    F["Size heap appropriately\n(Xms = Xmx, 2–3x live set)"]
    G["Tune collector-specific flags\n(IHOP, regions, tenuring)"]
    H["Validate with production load\nand GC log analysis"]

    A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F --> G --> H

    style A fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style C fill:#e8933a,color:#fff
    style D fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style E fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style F fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style G fill:#7b68ae,color:#fff
    style H fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff

docs.title: Topic 3: Bytecode & JIT Internals
docs.text:
Book: Optimizing Java — Practical Techniques for Improving JVM Application Performance

Authors: Benjamin J. Evans, James Gough, Chris Newland (O'Reilly Media)

Part Covered: Part III — JIT Compilation (Chapters 9–10)

docs.title: Topic Structure
docs.text: Document Chapter Coverage Status  Chapter 9 — Code Execution on the JVM Ch 9 JVM as stack machine, bytecode opcode families (load/store, arithmetic, flow control, method invocation, platform), HotSpot template interpreter, JIT fundamentals (C1/C2/tiered), Code Cache, AOT vs JIT  Complete  Chapter 10 — Understanding JIT Compilation Ch 10 JITWatch tool, Method Data Objects (MDOs), inlining (gateway optimization), loop unrolling, escape analysis & scalar replacement, lock elision/coarsening, monomorphic dispatch, intrinsics, OSR, 8000-byte compilation wall  Complete

docs.title: Chapter 9: Code Execution on the JVM — Stack Machine, Bytecode & JIT Basics
docs.text: Establishes the JVM's fundamental execution model: a stack-based virtual machine where all computations happen on a per-method evaluation stack, not in CPU registers. Every JVM opcode pops operands from the stack, performs an operation, and pushes results back. Introduces bytecode as the intermediate representation produced by javac: architecture-neutral, platform-agnostic, and strictly big-endian. Each opcode is 1 byte (200 of 256 values used in Java 10). Covers the five opcode families: Load/Store (load, store, ldc, getfield), Arithmetic (iadd, dmul, fcmp), Flow Control (goto, if_icmpge, tableswitch), Method Invocation (invokevirtual, invokespecial, invokeinterface, invokestatic, invokedynamic), and Platform (new, monitorenter, monitorexit). Deep-dives into the five method invocation opcodes: invokevirtual (standard virtual dispatch through vtable), invokespecial (direct dispatch for private/constructors/super), invokeinterface (interface vtable lookup — slower), invokestatic (no receiver needed), and invokedynamic (runtime strategy pattern — powers lambdas in Java 8+). Explains why final methods use invokevirtual in bytecode for binary compatibility (JLS 13.4.17) but HotSpot uses an internal private opcode for fast direct dispatch. Introduces HotSpot's Template Interpreter — dynamically generated at JVM startup using native CPU assembly — as opposed to a slow switch-loop interpreter. Covers JIT compilation basics: Profile-Guided Optimization (PGO), why profile data is discarded at shutdown, On-Stack Replacement (OSR) for hot loops in otherwise-cold methods, and the 5-tier tiered compilation model (Tier 0 = Interpreter → Tier 4 = C2 aggressive). Explains the Code Cache as a fixed-size native memory region for compiled nmethods, and why exhausting it silently halts all JIT compilation.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Understanding JIT Compilation — Optimizations Deep Dive
docs.text: The definitive chapter on what the JIT actually does inside. Centers on JITWatch — an open-source JavaFX tool for inspecting JIT decisions, showing Java source, bytecode, and native assembly side-by-side. Covers inlining as the gateway optimization that enables everything else: by copying callee code into the caller, the JIT can then see escape analysis, dead code elimination, loop unrolling, and lock elision opportunities that were previously invisible. Inlining limits: MaxInlineSize (35 bytes, non-hot), FreqInlineSize (325 bytes, hot), MaxInlineLevel (9 call levels deep). Loop unrolling duplicates loop bodies to reduce back-branch frequency — works for int/short/char counters but NOT long counters, causing ~64% performance penalty for long-typed loops. Also enables bounds check elimination (split loop into pre/main/post sections; main section has no bounds checks). Escape Analysis: determines if an object escapes its defining method (NoEscape → scalar replace into registers, avoiding heap allocation entirely; ArgEscape → passes to inlined callee; GlobalEscape → must heap-allocate). Critical limit: arrays > 64 elements are NOT scalar replaced (configurable via -XX:EliminateAllocationArraySizeLimit). Lock optimizations: lock elision (remove locks on non-escaping objects), lock coarsening (merge adjacent synchronized blocks), nested lock elimination. Monomorphic dispatch: at monomorphic call sites (one receiver type observed), replaces vtable lookup with klass word check + direct branch — degraded at megamorphic sites (3+ types); recoverable via explicit instanceof type peeling. Intrinsics: pre-written architecture-specific assembly for core methods (System.arraycopy, AES, Math.log10, System.currentTimeMillis). The 8,000-byte compilation wall: methods > 8,000 bytes of bytecode are NEVER JIT-compiled — they run at interpreter speed forever (~50% performance).

docs.title: What You'll Master
docs.text:
• Stack Machine Model — How the JVM evaluation stack works vs CPU registers
  • Bytecode Opcode Families — Load/store, arithmetic, flow control, method invocation, platform
  • Method Invocation Semantics — invokevirtual vs invokespecial vs invokedynamic dispatch
  • Template Interpreter — HotSpot's dynamically-generated native-code interpreter
  • Tiered Compilation — 5 execution levels (Tier 0-4), C1 vs C2, compilation pathways
  • Code Cache — Fixed-size native code region; exhaustion silently kills JIT
  • JITWatch — TriView: Java source + bytecode + native assembly side-by-side
  • Inlining — The gateway optimization; size limits (MaxInlineSize, FreqInlineSize)
  • Loop Unrolling — Why int loops are 64% faster than long loops
  • Escape Analysis & Scalar Replacement — Stack allocation via object decomposition into scalars
  • Monomorphic vs Megamorphic Dispatch — Why 3+ receiver types kill call site performance
  • Intrinsics — Pre-built assembly implementations of core library methods
  • 8,000-Byte Wall — Never write methods > 8,000 bytes of bytecode

docs.title: Optimizing Java — Book Context
docs.text: Reading Group Chapters Topics Week 1 (Topic 1) 1–5 Foundations: observables, JVM anatomy, hardware, testing, statistics Week 2 (Topic 2) 6–8 Garbage Collection: algorithms, heap analysis, GC tuning Week 3 (This part) 9–10 Bytecode & JIT: stack machine, opcodes, inlining, escape analysis Week 4 11–12 Profiling & Concurrency: profilers, thread analysis, lock contention Week 5 13–15 Advanced JVM Optimization Techniques

docs.title: Key Internals to Understand
docs.text:
• Evaluation Stack vs CPU Registers — Why the JVM's stack architecture adds an extra abstraction layer that JIT must eliminate to produce efficient native code
  • invokedynamic Bootstrap Method — How lambda desugaring works: a CallSite object with a MethodHandle target is created once at first invocation; subsequent calls bypass the bootstrap entirely
  • Method Data Objects (MDOs) — Per-method profiling data structures (invocation counts, branch probabilities, observed receiver types at call sites) that C1 populates and C2 consumes for speculative optimization
  • Deoptimization — When a C2 guard fails (unexpected class type, branch probability changes), HotSpot must "deopt" the nmethod: mark it made not entrant, and re-interpret the method from the point of failure
  • Scalar Replacement Limit — Why the EliminateAllocationArraySizeLimit=64 default means a 65-element array allocates on the heap while a 64-element array gets register-allocated
  • Type Peeling for Megamorphic Sites — Adding an explicit instanceof check before a polymorphic call site to peel off the dominant type into a monomorphic fast path, leaving the remaining site bimorphic

docs.title: Chapter 10: Understanding JIT Compilation
docs.text:
Book: Optimizing Java — Practical Techniques for Improving JVM Application Performance

Authors: Benjamin J. Evans, James Gough, Chris Newland

Chapter: 10 — Understanding JIT Compilation (Optimizations Deep Dive)

Status: Complete

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • Use JITWatch's TriView to inspect inlining decisions and native assembly
  • Explain inlining as the gateway optimization and its size limits
  • Understand loop unrolling, why long loop counters defeat it, and bounds check elimination
  • Apply escape analysis to predict when objects will be stack-allocated (scalar replaced)
  • Explain the 64-element array scalar replacement limit and its benchmark consequences
  • Describe lock elision, lock coarsening, and nested lock elimination
  • Distinguish monomorphic/bimorphic/megamorphic call sites and apply type peeling
  • List key JVM intrinsics and understand why they matter
  • Know the 8,000-byte bytecode compilation wall and its consequences

docs.title: 1. JITWatch — Inspecting JIT Decisions
docs.text:
JITWatch (by Chris Newland, one of this book's authors) is an open-source JavaFX tool that makes JIT decisions visible:

# Required flags to generate log for JITWatch
java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions \
     -XX:+TraceClassLoading \
     -XX:+LogCompilation \
     -jar myapp.jar

docs.title: JITWatch Views
docs.text:
View Purpose Main Window Class tree, compiled methods, nmethod sizes, tier levels TriView Java source + Bytecode + Native Assembly side-by-side with annotations Sandbox Live prototyping — paste Java code, see JIT decisions in real-time Code Cache Layout Visual memory map of compiled nmethods by address JarScan Scans JAR files for methods exceeding inlining size limits

TriView Is the Key Tool

TriView shows inline annotations like: "Object of type int[] does not escape method. Heap allocation has been eliminated." — this directly confirms scalar replacement happened.

docs.title: 2. Inlining — The Gateway Optimization
docs.text:
Inlining copies the body of a callee method directly into the caller's call site, eliminating:

  • Parameter passing overhead
  • Method lookup indirection (vtable traversal)
  • Call stack frame creation
  • Return value transfer

But the real value is what inlining enables:

flowchart TD
    INLINE["Inlining\n(copies callee body into caller)"]
    EA["Escape Analysis\n(can now see object scope)"]
    DCE["Dead Code Elimination\n(can see unused branches)"]
    LU["Loop Unrolling\n(can see loop body context)"]
    LE["Lock Elision\n(can see lock scope)"]

    INLINE -->|"enables"| EA
    INLINE -->|"enables"| DCE
    INLINE -->|"enables"| LU
    INLINE -->|"enables"| LE

    style INLINE fill:#3d59a1,color:#fff
    style EA fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style DCE fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style LU fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style LE fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff

Inlining Is the Gateway

Almost every other JIT optimization depends on inlining having happened first. Escape analysis cannot prove an object doesn't escape if it passes through un-inlined call boundaries. Lock elision cannot prove a lock is thread-local if the method isn't inlined.

docs.title: Inlining Thresholds
docs.text: Flag Default Applies To -XX:MaxInlineSize=35 35 bytes Non-hot methods -XX:FreqInlineSize=325 325 bytes Hot (frequently invoked) methods -XX:InlineSmallCode=1000 1000 bytes Existing compiled code (non-tiered) -XX:InlineSmallCode=2000 2000 bytes Existing compiled code (tiered) -XX:MaxInlineLevel=9 9 levels Maximum call depth for recursive inlining

docs.title: Real-World Inlining Failure — String.toUpperCase()
docs.text:
In JDK 8, String.toUpperCase() is 439 bytes of bytecode — exceeds FreqInlineSize of 325. The JIT refuses to inline it. Solution: write a specialized ASCII-only version:

// JDK 8 String.toUpperCase() = 439 bytes → NOT inlined → slow

// Custom ASCII-only version = 69 bytes → inlined → fast
public static String toUpperCaseASCII(String s) {
    char[] chars = s.toCharArray();
    for (int i = 0; i < chars.length; i++) {
        if (chars[i] >= 'a' && chars[i] <= 'z') {
            chars[i] -= 32;
        }
    }
    return new String(chars);
}
// Result: 2.4x performance improvement purely from successful inlining

docs.title: Loop Unrolling
docs.text:
Loop unrolling duplicates the loop body N times, reducing the frequency of back-branches:

// Original loop (simplified)
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    sum += data[i];
}

// After 4x unrolling (JIT does this internally)
for (int i = 0; i < n - 3; i += 4) {
    sum += data[i];
    sum += data[i+1];
    sum += data[i+2];
    sum += data[i+3];
}
// Handle remaining elements in post-loop

docs.title: Why long Loop Counters Are Fatal
docs.text:
// FAST: ~30 M ops/sec — int counter enables unrolling
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) { ... }

// SLOW: ~11 M ops/sec — long counter defeats unrolling (64% slower!)
for (long i = 0; i < N; i++) { ... }

The Loop Counter Rule

Always use int, short, or char for loop counters. long counters are NOT unrolled by HotSpot. The performance penalty can be 64% — not a micro-optimization but a major architectural concern.

docs.title: Bounds Check Elimination (BCE)
docs.text:
Without BCE, every data[i] access requires a bounds check: if (i < 0 || i >= data.length) throw AIOOB. BCE eliminates these in the main loop body:

flowchart LR
    subgraph LOOP_STRUCTURE["Loop Split for BCE"]
        PRE["Pre-Loop\n(first few iterations)\nWith bounds checks"]
        MAIN["Main Loop (unrolled)\nBounds checks ELIMINATED\n+ Safepoint polls removed\n→ Maximum performance"]
        POST["Post-Loop\n(remaining tail)\nWith bounds checks"]
    end

    PRE --> MAIN --> POST

    style PRE fill:#e8933a,color:#fff
    style MAIN fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style POST fill:#e8933a,color:#fff

Safepoint poll removal: The main unrolled loop also has JVM safepoint polls removed — the JIT can prove the loop will terminate, so no mid-loop safepoint is needed.

docs.title: 4. Escape Analysis & Scalar Replacement
docs.text:
Escape analysis determines whether an allocated object can escape its defining method or thread:

flowchart TD
    ALLOC["Object Allocation\n(new Point(x, y))"]

    subgraph ESCAPE["Escape Categories (escape.hpp)"]
        NO["NoEscape (=1)\nDoes not escape method/thread\n→ Scalar Replacement eligible"]
        ARG["ArgEscape (=2)\nPassed as argument to callee\n(but callee doesn't store it)\n→ Eligible only if callee inlined"]
        GLOBAL["GlobalEscape (=3)\nStored to field or returned\n→ Must heap-allocate"]
    end

    ALLOC --> ESCAPE

    style NO fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style ARG fill:#e8933a,color:#fff
    style GLOBAL fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff

docs.title: Scalar Replacement — Stack Allocation Without a Stack
docs.text:
When an object is NoEscape, the JIT deconstructs it into its primitive fields:

// Source code
void compute() {
    Point p = new Point(x, y);  // heap allocation?
    double dist = Math.sqrt(p.x * p.x + p.y * p.y);
    // p is never returned or stored anywhere
}

// After escape analysis + scalar replacement:
// Point p is NEVER allocated on the heap
// p.x and p.y become CPU registers (or stack slots)
// No GC pressure — completely allocation-free!

docs.title: The 64-Element Array Limit
docs.text:
The Hidden Array Cliff

Arrays are also subject to escape analysis and scalar replacement, but only if they have ≤ 64 elements:

int[] arr63 = new int[63];   // → Scalar replaced! No heap allocation
int[] arr64 = new int[64];   // → Scalar replaced! No heap allocation
int[] arr65 = new int[65];   // → Heap allocated! 2.4x performance drop

Benchmark results from the book: - 64 elements: ~49.8 M ops/sec - 65 elements: ~21.1 M ops/sec (2.4x slower!)

Fix: -XX:EliminateAllocationArraySizeLimit=65 (or whatever your array size is)

docs.title: No Partial Escape Analysis
docs.text:
HotSpot uses whole-method escape analysis — if an object escapes on ANY code path (even an unlikely one), it's considered escaped on ALL paths:

void process(boolean flag) {
    List<String> results = new ArrayList<>();  // Escape analysis result?

    if (flag) {
        globalCache.put(key, results);  // ESCAPES on this branch!
    }

    // Even though results doesn't escape on the !flag branch,
    // HotSpot marks it ArgEscape/GlobalEscape everywhere
    // → Always heap-allocated
}

// Fix: Move the allocation inside the non-escaping branch
void process(boolean flag) {
    if (!flag) {
        List<String> results = new ArrayList<>();  // Local only — NoEscape!
        // ... use results locally
    } else {
        globalCache.put(key, new ArrayList<>());
    }
}

docs.title: 5. Lock Optimizations — Elision, Coarsening & Nested Elimination
docs.text: These optimizations apply only to intrinsic synchronized locks — not ReentrantLock or other java.util.concurrent locks.

docs.title: Lock Elision
docs.text:
If an object is NoEscape, its monitor is inaccessible to other threads. The JIT completely removes monitorenter/monitorexit bytecodes:

// Source
void doWork() {
    synchronized (new Object()) {  // Lock on a local object!
        compute();
    }
}

// JIT eliminates the lock entirely — it's a NoEscape object
// No synchronization overhead

docs.title: Lock Coarsening
docs.text:
Adjacent synchronized blocks on the same monitor are merged into one:

// Source
synchronized (lock) { operation1(); }
synchronized (lock) { operation2(); }  // Same lock!

// JIT merges into:
synchronized (lock) { operation1(); operation2(); }
// Eliminates redundant lock acquire/release pair

docs.title: Nested Lock Elimination
docs.text:
When the JIT can prove a thread already holds an outer lock on a static final object or this, inner synchronized blocks on the same object are eliminated:

synchronized (LOCK) {
    // JIT can see LOCK is already held
    synchronized (LOCK) {  // ← Eliminated by JIT
        innerWork();
    }
}

Flag to observe: -XX:-EliminateLocks (disables) / -XX:-EliminateNestedLocks (disables nested)

docs.title: 6. Monomorphic Dispatch — The Call Site Optimization
docs.text:
Virtual method calls (invokevirtual, invokeinterface) require vtable lookup at runtime. The JIT profiles call sites using Method Data Objects (MDOs):

flowchart TD
    subgraph SITES["Call Site Classification"]
        MONO["Monomorphic\n1 receiver type observed\n→ KlassWord check + direct branch\n(fastest)"]
        BI["Bimorphic\n2 receiver types observed\n→ 2 KlassWord checks cached\n(fast)"]
        MEGA["Megamorphic\n3+ receiver types observed\n→ Full vtable lookup\n(slow — no caching)"]
    end

    style MONO fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style BI fill:#e8933a,color:#fff
    style MEGA fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff

docs.title: Type Peeling — Recovering Megamorphic Call Sites
docs.text:
// Megamorphic call site (3+ types: Dog, Cat, Bird)
void handleAnimal(Animal a) {
    a.speak();  // → vtable lookup every time
}

// Type peeling — peel off dominant type
void handleAnimal(Animal a) {
    if (a instanceof Dog) {
        ((Dog) a).speak();   // Monomorphic — fast direct call
    } else {
        a.speak();           // Bimorphic (Cat + Bird) — still fast
    }
}
// Result: ~13% throughput improvement from the book's benchmark

When to Apply Type Peeling

Use type peeling when profiling shows a call site is megamorphic but one type overwhelmingly dominates. Explicitly checking that type transforms the remaining call site from megamorphic to bimorphic.

docs.title: 7. Intrinsics — Assembly-Optimized Core Methods
docs.text:
Intrinsics are pre-written, architecture-specific assembly implementations of selected core library methods that the JIT recognizes by name and replaces entirely:

Method What the JIT Does System.arraycopy() SIMD vectorized copy using MOVDQU/REP MOVSB System.currentTimeMillis() Direct rdtsc / OS fast path (no JNI overhead) Math.min() / Math.max() CMOV conditional move (branchless) Math.log10() fldlg2 + fyl2x FPU instructions directly AES encrypt/decrypt AESENC/AESDEC hardware AES instructions String.equals() Vectorized comparison Object.hashCode() Direct identity hash implementation

Annotated with @HotSpotIntrinsicCandidate in Java 9+ source code.

Intrinsics Are Why Java Can Match C++ Performance

For compute-intensive code using core library methods, HotSpot intrinsics ensure Java uses the same optimized CPU instructions as hand-written C. AES encryption in Java 9+ runs at native hardware speed.

docs.title: 8. On-Stack Replacement (OSR)
docs.text:
OSR solves the problem of hot loops inside cold methods (e.g., a long-running loop in main()):

public static void main(String[] args) {
    // Method 'main' is called once — invocation counter never triggers JIT
    // But this loop runs 10 million times — it's HOT!
    long sum = 0;
    for (long i = 0; i < 10_000_000; i++) {
        sum += i;
    }
    System.out.println(sum);
}

OSR process: 1. Back-branch counter in the interpreter increments on each loop iteration 2. When counter exceeds OSR threshold → compile the loop for C2 3. JIT compiles the entire method body around the loop 4. Execution transfers mid-loop from interpreted stack frame to compiled native frame 5. Subsequent iterations run at C2 speed

You can see OSR compilations in -XX:+PrintCompilation output as methods flagged with %.

docs.title: 9. The 8,000-Byte Compilation Wall
docs.text:
The Most Important Size Limit in Java Performance

Methods exceeding 8,000 bytes of bytecode (HugeMethodLimit) will NEVER be JIT-compiled — they execute in the interpreter indefinitely.

Performance impact: 

Method < 8000 bytes:  ~89,550 ops/sec (C2 compiled)
Method > 8000 bytes:  ~44,429 ops/sec (interpreter only)
2x performance penalty — permanent, silent, no warning in production.

docs.title: Who Hits the 8,000-Byte Wall?
docs.text:
• Generated code: ORM framework SQL builders (Hibernate Criteria, jOOQ)
  • Auto-generated parsers: ANTLR-generated parsers with large switch tables
  • Hand-written god methods: Business logic in 1,000-line methods
  • Deserialization code: Auto-generated readObject() / Protobuf deserialization

Detection with JarScan (bundled in JITWatch):

java -jar jitwatch.jar jarScan --mode=bc --limit 8000 myapp.jar
# Lists all methods > 8000 bytes — compile-wall candidates

Fix: Refactor large methods by extracting sub-methods. Each extracted method can independently cross its inlining threshold and be JIT-compiled.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Code Execution on the JVM
docs.text:
Book: Optimizing Java — Practical Techniques for Improving JVM Application Performance

Authors: Benjamin J. Evans, James Gough, Chris Newland

Chapter: 9 — Code Execution on the JVM (Bytecode, Interpreter & JIT Basics)

Status: Complete

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • Explain the JVM's stack-machine execution model and its three data areas
  • Read and interpret basic bytecode sequences produced by javac
  • Distinguish the 5 opcode families and the operations in each
  • Explain the 5 method invocation opcodes and when each is used
  • Describe HotSpot's Template Interpreter and how it differs from a switch-loop interpreter
  • Explain tiered compilation (Tiers 0-4), C1 vs C2, and the 4 compilation pathways
  • Explain the Code Cache and why exhaustion silently kills JIT compilation

docs.title: 1. The JVM as a Stack Machine
docs.text:
Unlike physical CPUs that operate on registers (named, fixed-size storage locations), the JVM executes bytecode as a stack machine:

flowchart LR
    subgraph JVM_DATA["Three JVM Data Areas (per method)"]
        ES["Evaluation Stack\nHolds operands &\nintermediate results\n(local to method)"]
        LV["Local Variables\nStores params &\nlocal vars\n(local to method)"]
        HEAP["Object Heap\nShared across all\nthreads & methods\n(objects & arrays)"]
    end

    style ES fill:#3d59a1,color:#fff
    style LV fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style HEAP fill:#e8933a,color:#fff

How a simple expression evaluates on the stack:

// Java source
int result = x + 3 + 1;

Step 1: iload x     → Stack: [x]
Step 2: iconst_3    → Stack: [x, 3]
Step 3: iadd        → Stack: [x+3]      (pops 3 & x, pushes sum)
Step 4: iconst_1    → Stack: [x+3, 1]
Step 5: iadd        → Stack: [x+4]      (pops 1 & x+3, pushes sum)
Step 6: istore result → Stack: []       (pops into local variable slot)

docs.title: 2. JVM Bytecode — The Architecture-Neutral IR
docs.text: javac compiles Java source to bytecode: a compact, platform-neutral intermediate representation interpreted by the JVM (and JIT-compiled to native code for hot paths).

docs.title: Bytecode Properties
docs.text: Property Detail Opcode size 1 byte per opcode (0–255; ~200 in active use) Endianness Strictly big-endian (MSB first) Typing Instructions are typed — iadd (int), dadd (double), fadd (float) Evolution Only 1 opcode added since Java 1.0 (invokedynamic); 2 deprecated (jsr, ret) Shortcut forms Common ops have argument-less shortcuts for compact class files (aload_0, iconst_0)

docs.title: Reading Bytecode with javap
docs.text:
javap -c MyClass.class       # Show bytecode
javap -verbose MyClass.class # Full constant pool + bytecode

docs.title: Family 1: Load & Store
docs.text:
Moves values between local variable slots, the constant pool, and the evaluation stack:

Opcode Operation iload i1 Push int local variable at slot i1 onto stack istore i1 Pop stack top into local variable slot i1 ldc c1 Push constant from Constant Pool index c1 aconst_null Push null reference (0-arg const shortcut) iconst_m1 Push integer -1 (0-arg const shortcut) getfield c1 Pop reference, push instance field value putfield c1 Pop value + reference, store into instance field getstatic c1 Push static field value (no receiver)

docs.title: Family 2: Arithmetic
docs.text:
Purely stack-based type-specific arithmetic — always pops operands, pushes result:

iadd, isub, imul, idiv, irem, ineg, ishl, ishr  (int)
ladd, lsub, lmul, ldiv, lrem, lneg              (long)
fadd, fsub, fmul, fdiv, frem, fneg              (float)
dadd, dsub, dmul, ddiv, drem, dneg              (double)
i2l, i2f, i2d, l2i, l2f, f2i, d2i, ...         (type casts)

docs.title: Family 3: Flow Control
docs.text:
Implements all branching and looping:

Opcode Operation goto i1 Unconditional jump to offset i1 if_icmpge i1 Pop two ints; jump to i1 if first ≥ second ifeq i1 Pop int; jump to i1 if == 0 tableswitch Dense integer switch (array lookup by index) lookupswitch Sparse integer switch (search through pairs)

docs.title: Family 4: Method Invocation ⭐
docs.text:
The most important family — every method call in Java compiles to one of five opcodes:

flowchart TD
    subgraph INVOKE["Method Invocation Opcodes"]
        IV["invokevirtual c1
Standard virtual dispatch
(instance methods, uses vtable)
Most common opcode"]
        IS["invokespecial c1
Direct/exact dispatch
(private methods, constructors,
super calls)"]
        II["invokeinterface c1
Interface vtable lookup
(slower — must search
interface method tables)"]
        IST["invokestatic c1
Static method dispatch
(no receiver object)"]
        ID["invokedynamic c1
Runtime bootstrap strategy
(lambdas, JRuby, Nashorn,
PatternMatching)"]
    end

    style IV fill:#3d59a1,color:#fff
    style IS fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style II fill:#7b68ae,color:#fff
    style IST fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style ID fill:#e8933a,color:#fff

Why final methods use invokevirtual

JLS 13.4.17 states that removing final from a method must not break binary compatibility. Therefore javac emits invokevirtual for final methods. However, HotSpot replaces this with an internal private opcode for fast direct dispatch — you get virtual syntax, direct-call performance.

docs.title: The invokedynamic Bootstrap Mechanism
docs.text:
invokedynamic (added in Java 7, used by Java 8 lambdas) enables a bootstrap method to determine the call target at first invocation:

// Lambda in source
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("hello");

// Compiled as invokedynamic → LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(...)
// At first invocation: Bootstrap creates a CallSite with a MethodHandle target
// At subsequent invocations: Direct dispatch — no bootstrap overhead

docs.title: Family 5: Platform (Memory & Sync)
docs.text:
Heap allocation and thread synchronization:

Opcode Operation new c1 Allocate new object of class at CP index c1 newarray prim Allocate primitive array anewarray c1 Allocate object reference array arraylength Get length of array on stack top monitorenter Acquire intrinsic lock (synchronized block entry) monitorexit Release intrinsic lock (synchronized block exit)

docs.title: 4. HotSpot Interpreter — Template-Based, Not Switch-Loop
docs.text:
A naive bytecode interpreter uses while(true) { switch(opcode) { ... } }. HotSpot does not do this:

flowchart LR
    subgraph NAIVE["Naive Switch Interpreter (slow)"]
        SW["while(true)\nswitch(opcode)\n  case IADD: ...\n  case ILOAD: ...\n  ...200 cases"]
    end

    subgraph HOTSPOT["HotSpot Template Interpreter (fast)"]
        TI["At JVM startup:\nGenerate native assembly\nfor each opcode using\ntarget CPU instructions\n& native OS stack frames"]
    end

    NAIVE -->|"Replaced by"| HOTSPOT

    style NAIVE fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff
    style HOTSPOT fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff

HotSpot generates a template — hand-written assembly snippets — for each opcode at startup. The templates exploit the native call stack and CPU registers directly, making interpreted execution significantly faster than a switch-loop approach.

docs.title: Safepoints in the Interpreter
docs.text: Between every 2 bytecodes, the interpreter checks the safepoint flag. This is the natural safepoint cadence — the evaluation stack is in a known, consistent state between opcodes.

docs.title: Why Not Ahead-of-Time (AOT)?
docs.text:
AOT Compilation JIT Compilation Compiles before execution Compiles at runtime for hot code Must be conservative — doesn't know runtime CPU features Can use all CPU features of the actual hardware No runtime profile data — must guess call frequencies Uses real profiling data (PGO) for speculative optimization One-time optimization opportunity Can re-optimize (deoptimize + recompile) as behavior changes

Profile Data Is Always Discarded

HotSpot discards all profile data on JVM shutdown. Why? Application behavior changes over time (e.g., a trading system on a high-volume news day behaves differently than on a quiet day). Using yesterday's profile for today's workload can degrade performance.

docs.title: JIT Compilation Units
docs.text:
• Normal JIT: Compiles a complete method when its invocation counter reaches threshold
  • On-Stack Replacement (OSR): Compiles a hot loop inside a cold method (e.g., a long-running loop in main()). Execution is transferred mid-loop from interpreted to compiled code.

docs.title: 6. Tiered Compilation — 5 Execution Levels
docs.text:
HotSpot's default execution model (since Java ⅞) uses 5 levels, managed by advancedThresholdPolicy:

flowchart LR
    T0["Tier 0\nInterpreter\n(profile collection\nbegins)"]
    T1["Tier 1\nC1 — full optimization\n(no profiling)"]
    T2["Tier 2\nC1 — invocation +\nbackedge counters"]
    T3["Tier 3\nC1 — full profiling\n(branch probs, types)"]
    T4["Tier 4\nC2 — aggressive\nspeculative optimization"]

    T0 -->|"0-3-4 (standard)"| T3 --> T4
    T0 -->|"0-4 (non-tiered)"| T4
    T0 -->|"0-2-3-4 (C2 busy)"| T2 --> T3 --> T4
    T3 -->|"0-3-1 (trivial)"| T1

    style T0 fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style T1 fill:#7b68ae,color:#fff
    style T2 fill:#7b68ae,color:#fff
    style T3 fill:#7b68ae,color:#fff
    style T4 fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff

docs.title: Compilation Pathways Explained
docs.text: Pathway Meaning 0 → 3 → 4 (standard) Normal hot method: Interpreter → C1 full profiling → C2 0 → 2 → 3 → 4 (C2 busy) C2 queue is backlogged; C1 quick compile buys time 0 → 3 → 1 (trivial method) Method is so simple C2 cannot produce better code than C1 0 → 4 (non-tiered) Legacy -server mode or explicit flag; skip C1 entirely

docs.title: C1 vs C2 Compilers
docs.text:
C1 (Client) C2 (Server) Speed Fast compilation Slow compilation (seconds) Output quality Moderate optimization Aggressive optimization Speculative opts No Yes (with guards) Internal IR SSA form Sea of Nodes Use case Desktop apps, quick startup Server apps, long-running

SSA (Single Static Assignment): Internal form where every variable is assigned exactly once. Treats all variables as effectively final, enabling a wide range of dataflow optimizations.

docs.title: 7. The Code Cache — JIT's Native Memory Region
docs.text:
The Code Cache is a fixed-size native memory region storing compiled nmethods (native methods — JIT output) and JVM internal stubs:

flowchart TD
    subgraph CACHE["Code Cache Structure"]
        UNALLOC["Unallocated Area\n(grows as new nmethods compiled)"]
        FREELIST["Free List\n(fragmented space from\nevicted intermediate compilations)"]
        SWEEPER["Sweeper Thread\n(reclaims evicted nmethods)"]
    end

    EVICTION["Eviction Triggers:\n- Method deoptimized\n- Higher-tier nmethod replaces C1\n- Class unloaded"]

    EVICTION --> FREELIST

    style UNALLOC fill:#4caf7c,color:#fff
    style FREELIST fill:#e8933a,color:#fff
    style SWEEPER fill:#4a6fa5,color:#fff
    style EVICTION fill:#dc5c59,color:#fff

docs.title: Code Cache Sizing
docs.text:
Condition Default Size Tiered compilation (Java 8+) 240 MB No tiered compilation 48 MB 
# Tune the code cache
-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=512m

Code Cache Exhaustion — The Silent JIT Killer

When the Code Cache fills up, HotSpot silently stops all JIT compilation. Application code reverts to running in the interpreter (~10x slower). You'll see this in logs as: 

VM warning: CodeCache is full. Compiler has been disabled.

Rule: "Any method that wants to compile should be given the resources to do so." Keep the code cache large enough that it never fills.

docs.title: Logging JIT Compilation
docs.text:
# Basic JIT log
-XX:+PrintCompilation

# Output format:
#  timestamp  id  tier  method name         bytes  code-size
    284    1    n 0     java.lang.Object::hashCode (0 bytes)
   1042    2    3       com.example.MyClass::process (45 bytes)
   2841    2    4       com.example.MyClass::process (45 bytes)
   3010    2           com.example.MyClass::process  made not entrant

# Flags in output:
#   n = native method
#   s = synchronized method  
#   ! = has exception handlers
#   % = OSR compilation
#   'made not entrant' = deoptimized/invalidated

docs.text:

docs.text:
Book: Optimizing Java — Practical Techniques for Improving JVM Application Performance

Authors: Benjamin J. Evans, James Gough, Chris Newland (O'Reilly Media)

Part Covered: Part IV — Performance Tooling (Chapters 11–12)

docs.title: Topic Structure
docs.text: Document Chapter Coverage Status Chapter 11 — Java Language Performance Techniques Ch 11 Collection internals (ArrayList vs LinkedList, HashMap bucket layout, treeifying, TreeMap), domain object memory leak diagnosis, finalization lifecycle & flaws, try-with-resources, Method Handles vs reflection Complete Chapter 12 — Concurrent Performance Techniques Ch 12 Amdahl's Law, JMM (happens-before, release-before-acquire), sun.misc.Unsafe, CAS & lock-free atomics, spinlocks, ReentrantLock/ReadWriteLock/Semaphore, ConcurrentHashMap, ForkJoinPool work-stealing, parallel streams, LMAX Disruptor, Actor model Complete

docs.title: Chapter 11: Java Language Performance Techniques — Collections, Memory & Method Handles
docs.text: A practical deep-dive into the performance characteristics of core Java language constructs — the data structures and APIs you use every day, but rarely understand at the memory and allocation level. Opens with the fundamental tension: Java stores reference-type fields as heap pointers (unlike C++ which can embed objects inline), which means every collection element is an indirection — and Object Layout / Project Valhalla are the long-term answer. Covers the two collection categories: sequential containers (index-based: ArrayList, LinkedList) and associative containers (hash/comparison-based: HashMap, TreeMap). ArrayList is backed by a contiguous array (pointer-bump allocation, O(1) indexed access, O(n) insert-at-head) — key insight: pre-size it with new ArrayList<>(expectedSize) or ensureCapacity() to avoid costly resizing (copy entire backing array). LinkedList has O(1) append/head-insert but O(n) indexed access — JMH benchmarks show beginLinkedList at 559 ops/ms vs beginArrayList at 3.4 ops/ms for head insertion, but accessArrayList at 269,568 ops/ms vs accessLinkedList at 0.86 ops/ms for indexed access. HashMap internals: bucket array + linked Node chains; spread function applies Shannon's Strict Avalanche Criteria; default capacity 16, load factor 0.75 — set initialCapacity = maxElements / loadFactor to avoid rehashing. When a bucket reaches TREEIFY_THRESHOLD, chains convert to red-black TreeNodes (O(log n) worst case but double memory per node). TreeMap for sorted/range queries. Diagnoses domain object memory leaks using jmap -histo: healthy heaps show only JDK types (char[], String, collections) in the top entries; domain objects in top 30 = memory leak or premature tenuring. Finalization deep-dive: unreachable objects with finalize() go to java.lang.ref.Finalizer queue, get run by the dedicated finalizer thread, then survive one extra GC cycle — nondeterministic, exception-swallowing, resurrection-prone — deprecated Java 9. try-with-resources: purely compile-time sugar via javac, deterministic block-scoped resource release, zero runtime overhead. Method Handles (java.lang.invoke): strongly-typed, signature-polymorphic direct method references via MethodHandles.lookup().findVirtual() — JIT-compilable with no boxing, vs reflection's Method.invoke(Object[]) which boxes all args.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Concurrent Performance Techniques — JMM, CAS, Locks & Fork/Join
docs.text: The comprehensive chapter on making concurrent Java code fast and correct. Starts from Herb Sutter's "The Free Lunch Is Over" (2005): CPU clocks plateaued at ~3 GHz; scaling now requires parallelism bounded by Amdahl's Law (T(N) = S + (T−S)/N — 5% serial code caps max speedup at 20×). The Java Memory Model (JMM) is a weak memory model (not all cores see changes simultaneously) defined via happens-before chains: synchronized creates Release-Before-Acquire, volatile creates synchronizes-with. volatile guarantees visibility but NOT atomicity — i++ is three bytecodes (getfield, iadd, putfield) and races even with volatile. sun.misc.Unsafe: the foundation of all lock-free JDK internals — allocateInstance(), compareAndSwapInt(), field offset arithmetic. CAS (Compare-And-Swap): single atomic CPU instruction; AtomicInteger wraps it in a retry loop; lock-free and deadlock-immune but degrades under high contention. Spinlocks: busy-wait via x86 xchg/test/jnz — eliminates context-switch overhead for ultra-short lock hold times, used by LMAX Disruptor. ReentrantLock (via AQS + LockSupport.park/unpark): CAS-based uncontended acquisition, interruptible, timed, fair/unfair modes. ReentrantReadWriteLock: multiple concurrent readers; exclusive writer — ideal for read-heavy caches. Semaphore: manages fixed permits; binary semaphore acts as mutex but any thread can release. ConcurrentHashMap: snapshot iterators, segment-level write locking, non-blocking reads. ForkJoinPool: work-stealing deque algorithm — idle threads steal from busy threads' tails; powers parallel streams via commonPool() (size = availableProcessors() - 1; beware NUMA/hyperthread anomalies). LMAX Disruptor: lock-free ring buffer using spinlocks and volatile variables; 4.87–8.70× faster than ArrayBlockingQueue across single/multi producer-consumer patterns. Actor model (Akka): isolated state + async immutable messages = no shared state, no deadlocks.

docs.title: What You'll Master
docs.text:
• Collection Performance Internals — ArrayList resizing, LinkedList node cost, HashMap bucket/treeify mechanics
  • HashMap Tuning — initialCapacity = maxElements / loadFactor prevents rehashing; treeifying = double memory
  • TreeMap vs HashMap — When sorted iteration, range queries, or subset operations justify O(log n)
  • Memory Leak Diagnosis — jmap -histo signatures, domain object tenuring, GC mark time inflation
  • Finalization Lifecycle — Why finalize() is deprecated; the one-extra-GC-cycle survivor problem
  • try-with-resources — Compile-time only; deterministic; zero GC cost; suppressed exceptions
  • Method Handles — Signature polymorphism, no boxing, JIT-friendly vs reflection's Object[] overhead
  • Amdahl's Law (Applied) — GC STW pauses and lock contention contribute to the serial fraction
  • JMM Guarantees — Happens-before, synchronizes-with, release-before-acquire; why volatile ≠ atomic
  • CAS Mechanics — AtomicInteger internals; lock-free but contention-sensitive
  • ReentrantLock Hierarchy — AQS, LockSupport, fair vs unfair, tryLock(), timed
  • ForkJoinPool Work-Stealing — Task subdivision, commonPool() sizing gotchas
  • LMAX Disruptor — Why spinlocks + ring buffer beats ArrayBlockingQueue by 5–9×
